lesson_title: Four Things That Make a Wire Fight Back
hook_text: Why is your kettle element thin nichrome, but the cable to your stove thick copper?
clip_script: Every wire resists the current a little, but how much depends on four things. First, the material. Copper is a smooth highway for electrons; nichrome is a bumpy dirt road with about sixty times more resistance. That is why house wiring is copper but kettle elements are nichrome. Second, length. A longer road means more bumps, so double the length and you double the resistance. Third, thickness. A wide road carries more traffic, so a thick wire has less resistance. That is why your stove and geyser need thick cables; a thin one would overheat. Fourth, temperature. Heat a metal and its atoms jiggle harder, so electrons crash into them more and resistance rises. Test it with a nichrome wire on a metre rule and an ammeter: slide the clip further along and watch the current drop. Just switch off between readings so the wire does not heat up.
visual_style: Electrons as cars on roads of different widths and surfaces; a nichrome wire on a metre rule with a sliding clip; an ammeter needle dropping; a glowing filament.
pacing: Hook question, four quick factors with visuals, then a hands-on demo finish.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson and plan a fair test for each factor.
